{{nihongo|'''Ishiura Shrine'''|石浦神社}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|abstract|Q845945|ar|جينجا|arz|ضريح شنتو|bcl|Shinto shrine|ca|Jinja|cs|Šintoistická svatyně|da|Shinto-tempel|de|Shintō-Schrein|el|Σιντοϊστικό Ιερό|eo|Ŝintoa sanktejo|es|Jinja|eu|Jinja|fa|معبد شینتویی|fi|Šintolainen pyhäkkö|fr|Sanctuaire shinto|hi|शिंतो मंदिर|hr|Šintoistički hram|hu|Sintó szentély|id|Jinja|it|Jinja|ja|神社|ka|ძინძია|ko|신사 (신토)|lb|Shintō-Schräin|mr|शिंतो मंदिर|nl|Jinja (heiligdom)|no|Jinja|or|ଜିଞ୍ଜା|pl|Jinja|pt|Templo xintoísta|ru|Дзиндзя|sc|Jinja|simple|Shinto shrine|sl|Šintoistično svetišče|sr|Шинтоистички храм|sv|Jinja|th|ศาลเจ้าชินโต|tok|tomo sewi pi nasin sewi Sinto|tr|Şinto tapınağı|uk|Святилище (синто)|uz|Dzindzya|vi|Thần xã|wuu|神社|zh|神社|zh_yue|神社|qid=Q845945}} in {{ill|Hondamachi|Q11520078|qid=Q11520078|lt=Honda-machi}}, {{ill|Kanazawa|Q191130|qid=Q191130}}, {{ill|Ishikawa Prefecture|Q131281|qid=Q131281}}. Its former shrine rank was prefectural shrine. At foundation it was called "Miw a Shrine"<ref name="chunichi20210503">[https://www.chunichi.co.jp/article/247613 New monument at Ishiura Shrine; 100 years since grandfather's donation] {{ill|Chunichi Shimbun|Q904678|qid=Q904678}}, viewed 2021-05-06.</ref>. It is a candidate for the small shrine "Miwa Shrine" in Kaga District, {{ill|Kaga Province|Q907469|qid=Q907469}}, in the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}, and is also said to be the oldest shrine in Kanazawa. {{nihongo|'''Ishiura Shrine'''|石浦神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Kaga Province]].

== Origin ==
Traditions include: clans of Miwa in {{ill|Kaga District, Okayama|Q1131574|qid=Q1131574}} built a shrine in the Nara period and invited Ōmononushi from {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|Q705542|qid=Q705542}} in {{ill|Yamato Province|Q907495|qid=Q907495}} as "Miwa Shrine"; or it was founded by imperial order in {{ill|Tenpyō|Q1199879|qid=Q1199879}} 11 ({{ill|739|Q23588|qid=Q23588}}); or by order of {{ill|Emperor Kazan|Q361000|qid=Q361000}}; or it began as Hase Kannon Hall in Ishiura, founded in Yōrō years (717-723) by a woman of the Matsuura clan inviting Hase Kannon of Yamato's Hase-dera. Although various theories exist, it was revered as the sōsha of seven villages of Ishiura-gō in Kaga District and considered the shikinaisha listed as "Miwa Shrine" among 13 seats of Kaga District under the Engi system<ref>Another candidate shrine is {{ill|Miwa Shrine (Q11357406)|Q11357406|qid=Q11357406|lt=Miwa Shrine}} in Tsubata, Kahoku District.</ref>.

With the rise of honji-suijaku-based shinbutsu shūgō, because the invited Ōmononushi was considered identical with the deity of {{ill|Hiyoshi Taisha|Q656451|qid=Q656451|lt=Hiyoshi Shrine}} in {{ill|Ōmi Province|Q843882|qid=Q843882}}, this shrine came to be called "Ishiura Sannō" or "Jinushi Gongen." Also, because the principal image of Ōmiwa's jingūji {{ill|Jingū-ji|Q1074971|qid=Q1074971}} was eleven-headed Kannon, this shrine's honji-butsu was also treated as Jūichimen Kannon; it was called "Yamato Hase Kannon," later "Hasezan Jikōin" by late Kan'ei years, and served by bettō temple clerics.

The original site (Nara-period foundation) is said to have been in Shimo-Ishiura village (around present Nagamachi 3-ban-chō), with traditions placing it in districts of samurai estates in the Edo period. In the Muromachi period there was a large shrine building there. In {{ill|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|Q1145058|qid=Q1145058}} 8 ({{ill|1580|Q6712|qid=Q6712}}), when {{ill|Sakuma Morimasa|Q986345|qid=Q986345}} attacked Kanazawa Gobō, base of the Kaga Ikkō-ikki, the shrine burned completely. The sacred body and Buddhist image had been jointly enshrined then; the honji Jūichimen Kannon was first placed at Atago-sha in Yamazaki village of Kodatsuno, then moved to Kannon-in on Utatsuyama. In {{ill|Keichō|Q1328185|qid=Q1328185}} 6 ({{ill|1601|Q6725|qid=Q6725}}), Maeda Toshinaga granted over 600 tsubo at Honda-machi; next year (March 29), shrine buildings were rebuilt at the former Ishiura fort site in Kami-Ishiura village and the shrine returned to Ishiura. In {{ill|Genna|de|Genna (Ära)|es|Genna|fa|گننا|fr|Ère Genna|id|Genna|it|Genna|ja|元和 (日本)|ko|겐나|ru|Гэнна|simple|Genna|sr|Гена|sv|Genna|tr|Genna|zh|元和 (日本)|qid=Q635245|lt=Genna}} 1 ({{ill|1615|Q6784|qid=Q6784}}), the land was incorporated into the lower residence of domain elder {{ill|Honda Masashige|Q11520055|qid=Q11520055}}. In Kanpō 3 ({{ill|1743|Q7580|qid=Q7580}}), another 170 tsubo were added, totaling over 770 tsubo.

Records in ''Kokujizasshō'' (letter from Jikōin, 1709) describe enshrined triad correspondences of Sannō Gongen and associated honji-butsu. Parishioner area covered seven Ishiura-gō villages and extended from around Musashigatsuji to the left bank of the Saigawa in present Kanazawa, a broad area. Thus the shrine was revered both as ubusuna of Kanazawa castle town and as castle guardian by successive Kaga lords. Toshinaga rebuilt its halls; under fifth lord Tsunanori, safe childbirth prayers were offered for his wife, strengthening faith in the shrine as a deity of safe delivery. The 50,000-koku Honda family also treated it as a prayer site, making repeated donations and reconstructions.

Originally the shrine enshrined Ōmononushi as Miwa Shrine, but the prominence of honji-butsu Jūichimen Kannon and the common name Jikōin led people to recognize it as a temple, and other shrines emerged claiming the Miwa name and shikinaisha status. However, it is argued to be clear this shrine is the Engishiki Miwa Shrine because ''Kaga no Kuni Shikinaisha Kyūshaki'' copied in 1653 records: "Miwa Shrine, one seat in Engishiki, located at Ishiura village of Ishiura-gō, called Ishiura Sannō, sōsha of seven villages of Ishiura-gō, now in Ishikawa District."

In the late feudal era, though affectionately called Ishiura Sannō / Jinushi Gongen / Jikōin, after the Meiji shinbutsu separation decree it was renamed "Ishiura Shrine" in Dec 1868 after the parish area name; in Sep 1880 it moved from Shimo-Honda-machi to its current address.

== Festivals ==
* {{ill|October 2|Q2932|qid=Q2932}} 10:00 - annual festival
There are over 50 festivals yearly (major, medium, minor). At the pre-Setsubun festival in {{ill|2020|Q25337|qid=Q25337}}, sumo wrestler {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ishiura}} (same surname as shrine name) was invited<ref>{{Cite news|url = https://www.hokurikushinkansen-navi.jp/pc/news/article.php?id=NEWS0000023048|title = Kanazawa Ishiura Shrine bean-throwing with sumo wrestler Ishiura|publisher = Hokuriku Shinkansen Tourism Navi (Hokkoku Shimbun)|date = 2020-02-03|accessdate = 2020-04-26}}</ref>.

== Stone monuments ==
A stone monument reading "Ishiura Shrine" was erected beside the approach in 1921<ref name="chunichi20210503" />. In 2021, another monument reading the original name "Miwa Shrine" was erected beside it<ref name="chunichi20210503" />.

== 101 Torii ==
[[File:101Torii.jpg|thumb|101 Torii]]
In {{ill|2019|Q25274|qid=Q25274}}, Ishiura Shrine built 101 torii on the north side of the precinct<ref name="hokushin">{{Cite news|url = https://www.hokurikushinkansen-navi.jp/pc/news/article.php?id=NEWS0000022621|title = 101 torii lined up at Ishiura Shrine, new symbol completed|publisher = Hokuriku Shinkansen Tourism Navi (Hokkoku Shimbun)|date = 2019-12-24|accessdate = 2020-04-26}}</ref><ref name="minkei">{{Cite news|url = https://kanazawa.keizai.biz/headline/3347/|title = 101 torii at Ishiura Shrine become new Kanazawa landmark|publisher = Kanazawa Keizai Shimbun|date = 2020-01-14|accessdate = 2020-04-26}}</ref>. Nicknamed "101 Torii," they were developed over half a year from July in commemoration of the Reiwa era change<ref name="hokushin"/> and enthronement of Emperor Naruhito<ref name="minkei"/>. The walking route is about 50 m<ref name="hokushin"/> and is illuminated at night. It has become a topic on social media such as Instagram<ref name="hokushin"/><ref name="minkei"/>.
